passage:
"Jomon, tell us what you found in the garden," said Yamini Miss.
Jomon held up his leaf. "A pillarcater!"
The class burst out laughing. "Pillarcater!" someone squealed.
Jomon's ears went pink and he pulled the leaf to his chest.
"Everyone is learning," said Yamini Miss. "I mix up long words too. Want to try again, Jomon?"
Jomon peeked at the giggling faces. The word did sound funny. A small smile crept up. "Pillarcater," he said slowly, and giggled too.
"Cat-er-pil-lar," Yamini Miss said with him.
"Caterpillar!" This time everyone laughed together, and Jomon laughed loudest.

qa.q: What did Jomon call the creature on his leaf?
qa.a: He called it a "pillarcater".

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when the class burst out laughing?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and small: his ears went pink and he pulled the leaf to his chest.

qa.q: Which choice helped Jomon, and why?
qa.a: Yamini Miss saying that everyone is learning, and Jomon choosing to giggle at the funny word, turned the laughter into something shared instead of hurtful.

qa.q: How might Yamini Miss see the first burst of laughter?
qa.a: She seems to notice it could hurt Jomon, so she reminds the class that she mixes up words too and gives him a kind second try.

grounding: A child mispronounces a word and the class laughs; a teacher says everyone is learning, and he chooses to laugh gently so the class laughs together.

passage:
Note from the class teacher, Tuesday.
During morning circle Sahil read the word of the day, "vegetable", as "veg-e-table". Divyansh shouted, "A table of veg!" and half the circle laughed. Sahil went red, pressed his lips together and slid behind the child next to him.
I paused the circle and said, "Everyone is learning. I still trip on words." I asked Divyansh how the joke might feel to Sahil.
At the water tap later, Divyansh started the joke again. I heard Sahil say, "That is unkind." Divyansh stopped. I told Sahil it was brave to speak up, and I will keep an eye on the group.

qa.q: Which word did Sahil read as "veg-e-table"?
qa.a: The word of the day, "vegetable".

qa.q: How can you tell Sahil felt hurt by the laughter?
qa.a: He went red, pressed his lips together and slid behind another child, which shows he felt small and embarrassed.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped the circle?
qa.a: The teacher paused the circle, said everyone is learning, and asked Divyansh how the joke might feel to Sahil.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have noticed when Sahil said "That is unkind"?
qa.a: Divyansh stopped straight away, so the joke may have looked less like shared fun and more like something that hurt Sahil.

grounding: A classmate mocks a child's mispronounced word; the adult says everyone is learning and the child says "that is unkind".

passage:
Monday. Sachin wobbled on his new cycle in the building's play area and toppled into the sand. The big kids laughed, so Pema laughed loudest of all. Walking home, her tummy felt funny and she did not skip.
Wednesday. At bath time Pema told Mama, "I laughed when Sachin fell." Mama rinsed her hair and asked, "How would you feel if you fell and everyone laughed?" Pema remembered slipping on the stairs and crying. "Bad," she whispered.
Saturday. Sachin wobbled and fell again. A giggle started behind her. Pema shut her mouth tight, ran over and asked, "Are you hurt?"

qa.q: Where did Sachin fall off his cycle?
qa.a: In the building's play area, into the sand.

qa.q: How did Pema feel after laughing at Sachin on Monday?
qa.a: She felt uneasy: her tummy felt funny and she did not skip on the way home.

qa.q: What helped Pema change what she did?
qa.a: Mama asked her how she would feel if everyone laughed at her, and she remembered crying after slipping on the stairs.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sachin when Pema runs over on Saturday?
qa.a: He may feel less alone and less silly, because one person is asking if he is hurt instead of laughing.

grounding: A child laughs at a fallen child because the big kids do, feels uneasy, and after a parent asks how she would feel, she stops copying the laughter.

passage:
Rain had kept the whole class inside, and the hall floor was slippery with muddy shoe prints. Yogesh ran for the ball, slid, and landed flat on his bottom. Laughter bounced off the walls. Abhinav laughed too, loud, glancing round to check the others were laughing. Then he saw Yogesh's chin wobble, and his own laugh went thin.
Asha Ma'am was busy mopping by the door, but she put the mop down and came over. "Abhinav, if you slipped and everyone laughed, how would you feel?"
Abhinav looked at his sandals. "Sad," he mumbled. He held out a hand to Yogesh. "Sorry. Come play on the dry side."

qa.q: Why was the hall floor slippery?
qa.a: It was slippery with muddy shoe prints because the rain had kept the class inside.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's thin laugh suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests he felt uneasy once he saw Yogesh's chin wobble, even though laughing with the group had felt fun at first.

qa.q: How did Asha Ma'am's question help, even on a busy day?
qa.a: She stopped mopping to ask how he would feel, which let Abhinav think about Yogesh and choose to say sorry and help.

qa.q: How might Yogesh see the moment Abhinav held out a hand?
qa.a: Yogesh may feel that someone noticed he was hurt, which could ease some of the embarrassment of falling in front of everyone.

grounding: A child copies the group and laughs at a classmate who fell, feels uneasy, and after an adult asks how he would feel, he apologises.

passage:
Monday. Karthik Sir held up Chandrika's page. "Look, she wrote her C backwards. Stand up, Chandrika, show everyone." She stood, face burning, eyes filling, while the class stared.
Tuesday. Chandrika would not put on her shoes. "I don't want school," she told Amma, and then all of Monday came out in sobs. Amma held her close. "It is not your fault. Mistakes are how we learn letters." That afternoon Amma went to talk with the head teacher.
Friday. Chandrika wrote a backwards C again. Karthik Sir knelt by her desk and quietly drew it the right way with her. She kept writing.

qa.q: What mistake did Chandrika make on her page?
qa.a: She wrote her C backwards.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she had to stand in front of the class?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and close to tears: her face was burning and her eyes were filling while everyone stared.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped?
qa.a: Amma listened, told Chandrika the mistake was not her fault, and went to talk with the head teacher that afternoon.

qa.q: How is Friday different for Chandrika from Monday?
qa.a: On Friday Karthik Sir helps her quietly at her desk instead of showing her mistake to the class, so she feels safe enough to keep writing.

grounding: A teacher makes a young child stand and show her mistake; she tells her parent, who says it is not her fault and speaks to the school, and later the teacher corrects her gently.

passage:
"Arnab, bring your spelling sheet up here," said Vidya Ma'am. She pointed at each red cross while the class watched. Arnab's neck went hot. He blinked hard so he would not cry.
At home, Mama was working late, and Arnab sat by the window with his sheet folded small in his pocket. He did not want dinner.
When the door opened at nine, he ran to her and it all spilled out.
Mama hugged him tight. "It is not your fault. Getting words wrong is how you learn them." Next morning she went with him to school and asked to see the head teacher.

qa.q: What was Arnab carrying in his pocket while he waited?
qa.a: His spelling sheet, folded small.

qa.q: Why did Arnab blink hard at the front of the class?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and close to tears while Vidya Ma'am pointed at his red crosses, and he was trying not to cry in front of everyone.

qa.q: What could a school do so children like Arnab feel safe making mistakes?
qa.a: Teachers could go over mistakes privately and kindly, and the head teacher can listen when a parent raises a worry like Mama did.

qa.q: How might Mama feel when Arnab tells her what happened?
qa.a: She may feel protective and sad for him, which is why she hugs him, tells him it is not his fault and goes to the school the next morning.

grounding: A teacher shames a young child by showing his mistakes; with his parent working late he holds it in, then tells her, and she reassures him and goes to the school.

passage:
Sumit reached for the plate of biscuits at Anirban Kaku's flat and knocked his mango juice straight onto the new cream sofa. The yellow puddle spread. Sumit froze. His eyes went to Baba, and his lip began to shake.
Baba did not frown. He crouched next to Sumit. "Accidents happen, shona. Let's clean it up together."
Anirban Kaku brought a cloth and a bowl of water. Sumit dabbed while Baba pressed. The stain faded to a pale mark.
"Sorry, Kaku," Sumit said.
"Thank you for helping," said Anirban Kaku. Sumit let out a big breath and leaned against Baba's arm.

qa.q: What did Sumit spill his juice on?
qa.a: His mango juice went onto the new cream sofa at Anirban Kaku's flat.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel just after the spill, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt scared and embarrassed: he froze, looked at Baba, and his lip began to shake.

qa.q: Why did Baba's reaction work well?
qa.a: Baba stayed calm, said accidents happen and cleaned up with Sumit, so Sumit could say sorry and help mend it instead of hiding in shame.

qa.q: How might Anirban Kaku see Sumit after the clean-up?
qa.a: Anirban Kaku seems to see a child who made an accident right, and thanks him for helping rather than dwelling on the stain.

grounding: A young child spills juice at someone else's home, and his parent calmly says accidents happen and they clean up together, so he feels relieved.

passage:
"Oh no!" Chetan's elbow hit the glass. Orange juice ran across Omkar Uncle's shiny floor and onto Chetan's shirt.
"I didn't mean it," Chetan whispered. His eyes filled.
"I know you didn't," said Mumma, kneeling. "Accidents happen. Let's clean up together, okay?"
"Everyone is looking."
"That's fine. Grab that paper napkin. You do this side, I'll do that side."
Omkar Uncle handed them more napkins. "My daughter spilled a whole jug here last week," he said with a grin.
Chetan wiped hard. "Is it gone?"
"All gone," said Mumma. Chetan smiled and reached for his biscuit again, more carefully this time.

qa.q: Whose floor did the orange juice spill on?
qa.a: It spilled on Omkar Uncle's shiny floor.

qa.q: What was Chetan worried about after the spill?
qa.a: He was worried that he was in trouble and that everyone was looking at him; his eyes filled and he said he didn't mean it.

qa.q: What made Mumma's response a wise one?
qa.a: She knelt beside him, said accidents happen and gave him a job in the clean-up, which turned his shame into fixing things.

qa.q: Why might Omkar Uncle tell the story about his daughter's jug?
qa.a: Omkar Uncle probably wants Chetan to feel less embarrassed by showing that spills happen to everyone.

grounding: At a host's home a child spills juice, and his parent says accidents happen and cleans up with him, easing his embarrassment.

passage:
Monday. Rice fell off Preeti's plate. "Why can't you eat neatly like Irawati?" Mummy sighed. Preeti glared at her big sister and later hid Irawati's favourite hair clip under the bed.
Wednesday. Irawati found the clip and cried. Preeti shouted, "Mummy loves you more!" Mummy went very still, then sat on the floor with Preeti. "I was wrong to compare you. It is not your fault, and it is not Irawati's either."
The next week. Mummy watched Preeti water every pot on the balcony without being asked. "You remember every plant," she said. Preeti grinned and showed Irawati which one had a new bud.

qa.q: Where did Preeti hide Irawati's hair clip?
qa.a: Under the bed.

qa.q: Why did Preeti shout that Mummy loves Irawati more?
qa.a: She felt less loved and angry after being compared with her sister, and the hurt came out at Irawati.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped?
qa.a: She said sorry for the comparison, told Preeti it was nobody's fault, and later praised Preeti for her own strength with the plants.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel about being held up as the example?
qa.a: Irawati may feel confused and hurt, since she did nothing wrong but lost her clip and got shouted at because of the comparison.

grounding: A parent compares a young child with her sister; the child feels less loved and angry at the sister until the parent stops comparing and values her own strength.

passage:
The school bus was due in five minutes, and Deepak still had one shoe on. Papa grabbed the lunch box. "Why can't you be ready like Sonali? She's been waiting at the door!"
Deepak threw the other shoe. "I hate Sonali!" His big sister looked at the floor.
Papa stopped. He knelt, even though the clock was ticking. "That was unfair of me. It's not your fault or Sonali's. You're slower in the mornings, but you're the one who found my lost keys yesterday."
Deepak sniffed and let Papa help with the laces. They ran for the bus together, all three of them.

qa.q: How many shoes was Deepak wearing when the bus was due?
qa.a: He had one shoe on.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he shouted "I hate Sonali"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry after being compared with his sister, and he aimed the anger at her.

qa.q: What did Papa do well, even in a rush?
qa.a: He stopped, knelt and admitted the comparison was unfair, then named something Deepak is good at, like finding the lost keys.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel when Deepak says he hates her?
qa.a: Sonali may feel hurt and confused, since she was only waiting at the door and did not choose to be compared.

grounding: In a morning rush a parent compares a boy with his sister; he feels angry at her, and the parent apologises and names the boy's own strength.

passage:
In the courtyard, Papa counted eggs into the basket. "Nirmala next door can count all the eggs already. Why can't you, Chandrika?"
Chandrika's cheeks went hot. She folded her arms and sat on the step with her back to him. "I won't count. Never."
Papa kept stacking eggs. Chandrika pushed her toe in the dust for a long time. Then she said, very small, "Papa, I feel sad when you say that."
Papa set the basket down. "You're right. I'm sorry, bitiya." He held out one egg. "Let's count together, just you and me."
She counted to twelve. Papa clapped. "Twelve! Yesterday it was eight."

qa.q: How far did Chandrika count with Papa?
qa.a: She counted to twelve.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel when Papa compared her with Nirmala?
qa.a: She felt hurt and stubborn: her cheeks went hot, she folded her arms and refused to count.

qa.q: What did Chandrika and Papa each do that helped?
qa.a: Chandrika said "I feel sad when you say that", and Papa apologised and counted with her, praising her own progress from eight to twelve.

qa.q: What might Papa realise when Chandrika speaks up?
qa.a: Papa may realise that comparing her with Nirmala made her want to stop trying, so he switches to praising what she did better than yesterday.

grounding: A father compares his daughter with the neighbour's child; she feels hurt and stubborn, says she feels sad, and he apologises and praises her own progress.

passage:
At the lake, Papa pointed along the jetty. "Look, Ines from next door already swims with her face in the water. Why won't you try, Jana?"
Jana climbed out, wrapped herself in her towel and sat on the warm boards. "I'm not swimming anymore."
Papa sat down next to her. Jana picked at the towel's edge. At last she said, "Papa, I feel sad when you talk about Ines."
"I'm sorry, Jana. That wasn't kind." He smiled. "Last week you wouldn't get your chin wet. Today you blew bubbles. That's your progress."
Jana let the towel drop and slid back into the water.

qa.q: Where did Jana sit after she climbed out of the lake?
qa.a: She sat on the warm boards of the jetty, wrapped in her towel.

qa.q: What does Jana wrapping herself in the towel suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt hurt and stubborn after being compared with Ines, and wanted to stop trying.

qa.q: What could other parents learn from Papa's second answer?
qa.a: They can apologise for a comparison and point to the child's own progress, like Jana going from a dry chin to blowing bubbles.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Jana said she felt sad?
qa.a: Papa may have felt sorry and a little surprised, because he quickly apologised and changed how he spoke to her.

grounding: A father compares his daughter with the neighbour's child at the lake; she feels hurt and refuses to try, tells him she feels sad, and he apologises and praises her own progress.

passage:
"Your peacock is so neat, Vidya," said Aparna. Every feather stayed inside the lines.
Aparna looked at her own peacock. Blue ran over the edges everywhere. She pulled her page onto her lap under the table.
"Aparna, where did your peacock go?" asked Neelam Ma'am.
"It's messy. Vidya's is better."
Neelam Ma'am pulled Aparna's first peacock from the folder. "Remember this one? One colour, all over the page. Look how far you have come."
Aparna looked at both. "I did the feathers green and blue this time," she said, and put her page back on the table.

qa.q: Where did Aparna hide her peacock?
qa.a: She pulled her page onto her lap under the table.

qa.q: Why did Aparna hide her page?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and a bit jealous, because Vidya's peacock stayed inside the lines while her own colours ran over the edges.

qa.q: What did Neelam Ma'am do that changed how Aparna felt?
qa.a: She showed Aparna her first peacock from the folder next to today's, so Aparna could see her own progress instead of Vidya's neatness.

qa.q: What might Vidya think when Aparna praises her peacock?
qa.a: Vidya may feel pleased by the praise and not know that Aparna is comparing and feeling bad about her own page.

grounding: A young child compares her colouring with the neater page of the girl beside her and hides it, until the teacher shows her how far she has come.

passage:
Note from the art teacher, Thursday.
We coloured mango trees today. Vinita sat beside Disha and kept glancing at Disha's page, which was very neat. Halfway through, Vinita stopped colouring, folded her page in half and pushed it into her bag. When I asked to see it, she shook her head and said Disha's was "the good one".
I took out Vinita's tree from June, a few green scribbles, and put it beside today's, with a brown trunk and leaves in two greens. I said, "Look how far you have come." Vinita unfolded her page and added orange mangoes. I will keep showing children their own old work.

qa.q: What did the class colour on Thursday?
qa.a: They coloured mango trees.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when she folded her page into her bag?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and discouraged, because she thought Disha's page was the good one and hers was not.

qa.q: How could a teacher help other children who compare like Vinita?
qa.a: A teacher could put the child's old work next to the new, as this teacher did, so the child sees their own growth.

qa.q: How might Disha see what happened at the table?
qa.a: Disha may not have noticed at all, since the comparison was happening quietly in Vinita's head and on Vinita's side of the table.

grounding: A child compares her colouring with a neater classmate's and hides it; the teacher shows her old work and says look how far she has come.

passage:
At the community centre's Saturday sports class, the coach blew the whistle and Yamini shot down the track like a bird. Kashish watched from the line, hands in fists. "I want to run like her," she whispered. Her face felt a bit hot too.
The coach crouched beside her. "You keep watching Yamini. Why not ask her?"
Kashish shuffled over. "Can you teach me to go fast?"
Yamini grinned. "Swing your arms like this, and look far ahead."
Kashish tried. She was not as quick, but she was quicker.
"Yamini is fast," said the coach. "And you, Kashish, can hop on one foot longer than anyone here."

qa.q: Where was the Saturday sports class held?
qa.a: At the community centre.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling as she watched Yamini run?
qa.a: She felt inspired and a little jealous; she whispered that she wanted to run like Yamini, with her hands in fists and her face hot.

qa.q: How did the coach help Kashish turn her feeling into something useful?
qa.a: The coach suggested she ask Yamini to teach her and then reminded her of her own strength, hopping on one foot.

qa.q: What might it be like for Yamini to be asked for help?
qa.a: Yamini may feel proud and happy to share, since she grins and shows Kashish how to swing her arms.

grounding: A young child sees another girl run fast, feels inspired and a little jealous, and with an adult's help asks her to teach her.

passage:
Tuesday. At the school race, Gurpreet flew past everyone, her plait bouncing. Madhav finished last and stood kicking the grass. "I want to run like her," he told his mother at pick-up, and scowled.
Thursday. Madhav's mother said, "Why don't you ask her? Maybe she can teach you." Madhav hid behind his mother's legs, then peeked out. "Gurpreet, can you teach me?" Gurpreet showed him how to lift his knees high.
Next Monday. Madhav practised knee-lifts all the way to the gate. He was still slower. But when Gurpreet's block tower kept falling, Madhav helped her. "You're good at running, I'm good at towers," he said.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet show Madhav on Thursday?
qa.a: She showed him how to lift his knees high.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Madhav have on Tuesday?
qa.a: He admired Gurpreet and felt a little jealous: he wanted to run like her but kicked the grass and scowled.

qa.q: What small step helped Madhav?
qa.a: His mother suggested he ask Gurpreet to teach him, which turned watching and scowling into learning from her.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when Madhav helps with her tower?
qa.a: Gurpreet may feel glad and see that they each have different things to share, just as she shared her running.

grounding: A young boy admires a girl who runs fast, feels a little jealous, asks her to teach him with his mother's help, and learns each child is good at different things.

passage:
"Mummy!" Gargi cried as the door closed. Her cheeks were wet.
Nirmala Ma'am knelt down. "Hello, Gargi. Mummy will come back after lunch. Will you hold my hand for a bit?"
Gargi sniffed and gave her hand.
"Do you like cooking? We have a little kitchen here."
"A real one?"
"A toy one. With a red kettle. Can you make me some tea?"
Gargi looked at the kettle. She poured pretend tea into a tiny cup and held it out.
"Mm, very hot," said Nirmala Ma'am, blowing on it.
Gargi almost smiled. "I'll make more," she said, and kept hold of the kettle.

qa.q: What colour was the kettle in the toy kitchen?
qa.a: It was red.

qa.q: How did Gargi's feelings change during the scene?
qa.a: She started scared and crying as the door closed, then felt a little safe as she held Nirmala Ma'am's hand and made pretend tea, almost smiling.

qa.q: What did Nirmala Ma'am do that helped Gargi settle?
qa.a: She knelt, said when Mummy would come back, held Gargi's hand and gave her a small job with the toy kettle.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Ma'am see a child crying on the first day?
qa.a: She seems to see it as normal, answering calmly with warmth and a simple game rather than asking Gargi to stop crying.

grounding: On her first day a child cries as her mother leaves; a warm teacher takes her hand and shows her the toys, and she feels a little safe.

passage:
Note from the nursery teacher, first day of term.
Minakshi arrived holding her mother's hand and cried loudly when her mother waved goodbye. She stood by the door with her fists at her eyes for several minutes. I knelt, took her hand and walked her slowly round the room: the sand tray, the dolls, the drum. At the drum she stopped crying and tapped it twice. Ritu, who started last month, brought over a second stick. By snack time Minakshi was sitting with Ritu and the drum. She cried once more at lunch, and I held her hand again. She will need a steady welcome tomorrow as well.

qa.q: What made Minakshi stop crying?
qa.a: At the drum she stopped crying and tapped it twice.

qa.q: How did Minakshi seem to feel at the start and by snack time?
qa.a: She seemed scared and sad at first, crying by the door, and a little safe by snack time, sitting with Ritu and the drum.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that other teachers could copy?
qa.a: The teacher knelt, took Minakshi's hand and walked her slowly round the toys, and held her hand again when she cried at lunch.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ritu to bring the second stick?
qa.a: Ritu, who started only last month, may remember feeling new and be happy to help someone else settle.

grounding: A young child cries on the first day as her mother leaves; the teacher takes her hand and shows her the toys until she feels a little safe.

passage:
Note from Kishore, class teacher, Monday and Tuesday.
Monday: At the gate Shankar held on to his mother's dress and cried. His mother kissed him, walked away, then came back three times to comfort him. Each time she returned, he cried harder. He cried most of the morning.
I spoke to her at pick-up about a short goodbye.
Tuesday: She hugged him once and said, "I will come when the lunch bell rings." Then she waved and left, without turning back. Shankar cried at the gate, but stopped by the time we reached the classroom. At lunch bell he ran to the gate and she was there.

qa.q: How many times did Shankar's mother come back on Monday?
qa.a: She came back three times.

qa.q: What does Shankar crying harder each time his mother returned suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the goodbye felt scarier and more confusing each time; his fear of her leaving grew instead of settling.

qa.q: What did Shankar's mother change on Tuesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: She gave one hug, told him when she would return and left without turning back, so the goodbye was short and clear.

qa.q: How might Shankar's mother have felt walking away on Tuesday?
qa.a: She may have felt torn and sad leaving him crying, but her waiting at the lunch bell showed him she kept her word.

grounding: A child clings to his mother's dress at the school gate; lingering makes it harder, while a short kind goodbye that says when she will return helps.

passage:
At the village school gate, Zubin gripped Ammi's dupatta in both fists and wailed.
Zeenat bent down. She could see the teacher waving the children in with the bell. It would be easy to slip away while Zubin watched the goats by the wall. She had done that once at her sister's house, and he had screamed for an hour.
So she stayed and looked into his eyes. "Zubin, I am going home now. I will come back when the school bell rings after lunch. Right here."
She hugged him once and walked away without looking back. At the wall, she heard his crying grow smaller.

qa.q: What was Zubin holding at the school gate?
qa.a: He gripped Ammi's dupatta in both fists.

qa.q: What was Zeenat worried about when she thought of slipping away?
qa.a: She worried he would feel tricked and frightened, remembering that he screamed for an hour when she sneaked away at her sister's house.

qa.q: Which choice did Zeenat make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She said a short kind goodbye and told him when she would come back, instead of sneaking off, so he could trust her.

qa.q: How might the goodbye feel to Zubin?
qa.a: Zubin still feels sad and cries, but because Ammi told him she was going and when she would return, his crying grows smaller.

grounding: A young child clings to his mother at the school gate; she chooses a short, kind goodbye with a clear return time instead of sneaking away.
